title: Unanswered prayer (2 Corinthians 12:7–9)
hookLine: Paul asked three times for a thorn to be removed, and it wasn't

cards: Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, admits he has something wrong with him. He doesn't say what. He calls it a thorn in the flesh.

And he prayed for it to go: "For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me." Thrice. Three times he asked, and three times, as far as we can tell, the thorn stayed exactly where it was.
The apostle writing this letter had a prayer that didn't get the answer he asked for.

teach.b: Paul calls it "a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me," and he never names it. Some readers guess an illness, or trouble with his eyes.
Others think it was a person, an opponent who kept dogging his work. Others think it was a temptation. Because Paul leaves it unnamed, some readers set their own thorn in that space.
Then the answer. It's not silence, and it's not yes: "And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The thorn stays.
What's promised instead is grace, enough of it, for living with the thing that didn't go away. Some Christians say every prayer gets an answer, and sometimes the answer is no.
Paul's story has a second half: no, and here is what will carry you. He isn't the only one who asked three times.

teach.h: GETHSEMANE: THE CUP DID NOT PASS.
teach.b: In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prays, "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." Matthew says he goes back and prays a third time, saying the same words.
And the cup doesn't pass. Paul's thorn and Jesus's cup sit side by side: real requests, honestly made, and a road that went on anyway. Notice, too, that Paul didn't stop after the first time.
Three tries before he heard the answer. Unanswered prayer, in this text, isn't prayer that failed.
It's prayer that was heard, and answered with something other than what was asked.

how: Christians keep praying for healing and help for themselves and others, and when an answer doesn't come, some turn to Paul's thorn and Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane, praying for grace to carry what remains.

o: a prayer said wrongly, so it didn't count
a prayer that gets no, but grace that is enough

the thorn was taken away after Paul's third prayer

in Matthew, Jesus prays a third time in Gethsemane
he prays the same words a third time, and the cup does not pass.

games.q: you're Paul. you've asked God three times to remove the thorn. what answer comes back?
o: my grace is sufficient for thee.
games.why: the thorn stays, and the answer is grace: my strength is made perfect in weakness.

practice: Name one thing that's stayed with you however much you've wanted it gone: a health problem, a hard relationship, a habit, a loss. Don't try to solve it.
If you pray, ask God about it once more, honestly, the way Paul did, and listen for what might carry you if it stays; if you don't, hold it, and ask what has helped you live with it so far.

wordCard.voice: Unanswered prayer. A prayer that seems to get no, like Paul's thrice-asked thorn, answered instead with grace that is enough.

orig.note: Greek: a thorn, or a sharp stake, the word Paul uses for his thorn in the flesh.

carryVoice: Your line: my grace is sufficient. The thorn stayed, and so did the grace. Same time tomorrow.
